title: Why holding a placard is terrorism, disruption in a balaclava is not
gist: A lawyer argues Britain has inverted its terrorism law: peaceful placard-holders are mass-arrested under proscription powers while organised balaclava-clad groups blockading Dover and Portsmouth ports face no arrests. The Supreme Court will soon hear the Palestine Action proscription appeal after the High Court and Court of Appeal split.

insights.claim: Recent English events show terrorism legislation being used to detain and prosecute peaceful protesters holding placards, while organised groups in black uniforms and balaclavas disrupting infrastructure are not arrested.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Enforcement asymmetry of this scale invites judicial correction and political backlash — a live UK legal and reputational risk.
insights.quote: terrorists peacefully hold placards and get immediately arrested, while protesters wear black uniforms and balaclavas and disrupt infrastructure and do not get arrested
insights.locator: Recent events in England now reveal

insights.claim: The root cause identified is that British politicians have stopped taking terrorism legislation seriously and ministers have got into the habit of misusing terror laws against easy targets.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Predicts continued mis-targeting: powers drift toward whoever is cheapest to police, not toward the highest actual threat.
insights.locator: The reason is that for some time British politicians

insights.claim: Anti-terrorism policy is described as topsy-turvy because ministers and police prefer easy targets under sweeping laws that seem even to confuse judges, producing mass arrests for holding signs and no arrests for political uniforms causing havoc.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: A diagnostic for state capacity: sweeping statutes plus discretionary policing reliably misallocate enforcement.

themes.theme: Palestine Action proscription and the courts

insights.claim: The proscription of Palestine Action is called the low point, because it criminalised anyone merely expressing support for the group even though its activists were already being prosecuted under ordinary criminal law for criminal damage.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Establishes the redundancy argument that the Supreme Court will have to weigh: existing criminal law was already sufficient.
insights.locator: The low point, of course, was the proscription of Palestine Action

insights.claim: Proscription extends beyond funding and organisational powers to criminalise speech-acts, giving police powers to arrest and courts to convict people merely for expressing support.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: The speech-act reach of proscription is the specific legal exposure that makes mass arrests possible and the appeal consequential.
insights.locator: Proscription has legal effects further up and down the chain.

insights.claim: The courts have split: the usually deferent High Court found against the government's proscription of Palestine Action at first instance, and the Court of Appeal then ruled it lawful partly on the ground that those arrested could protest about other things if they wanted.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: A first-instance loss for government reversed on appeal on weak reasoning raises the odds of the proscription being unwound at the top court.
insights.locator: At first instance, the usually deferent High Court

insights.claim: The Supreme Court has decided to hear a further appeal on the Palestine Action proscription, with the most senior justices sitting soon.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: A dated legal catalyst: the ruling will set the boundary for UK protest proscription powers.
insights.locator: The Supreme Court has now decided to sort out this legal confusion

themes.theme: Organised street formations as emerging threat

insights.claim: The appearance of coordinated, intimidatingly clad groups online and on the streets cannot logically be spontaneous: uniforms and disguises by themselves point to planning in advance.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Premeditation is the legal hinge that would bring these groups within terror or public-order statutes — watch for the first such charges.
insights.quote: These are not and logically cannot be spontaneous demonstrations. The uniform and disguises by themselves point to planning in advance.

insights.claim: “Stop the boats” groups appeared in Dover and Portsmouth and sought to cause disruption and block ports, and the police, adept at arresting scores of peaceful protesters under terror laws, appear to have had no advance intelligence and were taken by surprise.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Intelligence failure around port blockades is an operational risk to UK freight and cross-Channel logistics.
insights.locator: Last week such “stop the boats” groups appeared

insights.claim: Just Stop Oil activists received long sentences for merely discussing blocking infrastructure, while balaclava-wearing gangs now do much the same with apparent impunity — something the author says one could almost call two-tier justice.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: A sentencing disparity this stark is politically combustible and likely to be litigated or reversed.
insights.quote: One could almost call it two-tier justice.

insights.claim: Terrorism law is meant to be the special body of law granting the state extra powers beyond the general law, used sparingly and deliberately, and historically enacted only on a temporary basis even against the IRA — whereas now it is used casually and inefficiently.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: The temporary-powers norm has been abandoned; permanent emergency powers are now the UK baseline, raising civil-liberties and legal-challenge risk.
insights.locator: Terrorism law is the special body of law
